title: Passages (2023) and the Startling Lack of Character

commenti.body:
I think it would have been better as a short(er) film, in part because of the scant characterization. The director/writer seems technically gifted and does scenes well—the last scene is a standout—but the screenwriting and direction is somewhat weak. Further, Tomas and Agathe hooking up, or even having an extended fling is believable but them having an LTR or entertaining a pregnancy is less so. I'm American not French but it seems to me the American director's take on French people borders on caricature what with the emphasis on cooking and eating together, perhaps most notably in Agathe's mother explaining to Tomas why the dinner is so important. [paraphrasing] 'We need to know you, to know that you will contribute and be there for our daughter, and to know you we must eat with you, ... '

If I'm being charitable, I would look at it as a comedy: Narcissism, The Movie. The manchild Tomas, smelling of sex and being late for an important dinner with Agathe's relatively 'traditional' parents was pretty funny. Up until the revelation of the abortion, Martin and Agathe are scarcely (if ever) shown to have interacted. Rather than a throuple, a 'bigamist' arrangement emerges, and Martin seems to see her as little more than a baby maker. His gift of a luxury item is almost like a financial payment for her reproductive services—it's one and done and less committal and time-intensive than actually spending time with her or helping her. He makes the news of the abortion about himself and his thwarted desires, despite his disappointment surely being insignificant next to her circumstances and feelings.

> Hannah Giorgis in The Atlantic says it "mak[es] poignant observations about power, desire, and the psychological contours of creative life" but I honestly don't see any such observations.

I mean, it wasn't my favorite movie or anything, but it was very much rich in those themes. They are all throughout the movie. 

Many of your criticisms of the film are really observations about the characters, and you're sort of mixing the two together, but they are oil and water. And in terms of character backstory, that doesn't need to be on the screen. A good performance has that attached. I found all three characters interesting, they reminded me of people I know, of situations I've been in, of paths taken and not taken, of marriages past. 

> Then there is Tomas himself, who we see hopping from one attraction to the next like a child at a carnival. He seems to have little self-control and even less care about the consequences until they hit him in the face.

That's the point. This is a movie about a man who hops from one attraction to the next and who has little self-control and cares not about consequences. To criticize the movie for being about what it is about seems strange (but maybe I am missing your point). It's like criticizing Tommy Lee Jones in The Fugitive because "Gerard is like a dog chasing a car, someone not at all interested in the innocence of Gimbal." Because that's what the movie is about, a determined FBI agent. This movie is about a man like you describe, who wants control over everything but introduces more than enough chaos to guarantee that he eventually will lose that control.

I share your feelings about this one. I saw and liked 4 of Ira Sachs previous films (especially Frankie!), and was looking forward to this, but came out wholly underwhelmed. 

The main reason was because the central dude was such an unsympathetic character, vain and flawed. The only wrinkle in this drama was the fact that the love triangle was between a gay couple and Adèle Exarchopoulos. 

Otherwise it was an utterly forgettable experience.

hmm.. what you said is true, but, somehow the subdued exploration of their characters really said a lot about them, for me atleast, it seemed that way.. 

They just felt more mature or practical, and though they were disturbed by Tomas' flip-flopping, they seemed to handle it all better, we do see their character development or their evolution out of Tomas' mess.. I also got the sense that, though they were stressed out and heart-broken, they kind of understood or expected it all from Tomas ("yeah, this isn't surprising"), however, weren't willing to entertain him in an effort to protect their own selves..  

And, we also see how Agathe from the beginning isn't really an expressive or articulate person, she seemed kind of closed off/kinda numb, emotionally. It felt like she was a person that fell silent during her turmoils.. (the scene where she hears Martin-Tomas in another room ,and she just silently lays on bed)... Adele's incredible performance showed a lot. And, for Martin as well, it was implied that this wasn't the first time Tomas cheated on him.. he was the calmer guy (atleast on the surface) when Tomas reveals his infidelity, and we see a range of emotions in him through the film, although yes, they were in connection to Tomas.. 

However, I thought all the characters' were well-portrayed, it's just that they were so different from each other and we get to know a lot about each of them, although on the face of it, it seems like the star of this movie was Tomas. But is he, really?

I don't need to have a ton of backstory but I felt that there was very little substance to Martin or Agathe. They barely get to talk since Tomas is always smothering them. I felt like I got to see how they react to Tomas' repeated bad choices and nothing else, which made the film tedious and boring, especially since the film is just their small arguments culminating in the total rejection of Tomas.  

>To criticize the movie for being about what it is about seems strange (but maybe I am missing your point). 

I see how that's the point in his character, my point is (admittedly not filled out very much, I wrote this in a burst after watching) that nothing about him is interesting beyond his childish behavior. Everyone around him tires of him and leaves, and he is just left to keep riding his bicycle? It felt like such an anticlimactic end, there isn't anything deeper to him. I just keep coming back to my title, I felt there wasn't any depth of character or dynamic interaction between any of the characters to build anything more than just "manchild acts like an ass, gets what's coming to him".

> They barely get to talk since Tomas is always smothering them

I get what you are saying, but acting is maybe 5% talking and 95% everything else. And they did the "everything else" really well IMO. Talking is the worst way to tell stories, generally, in film. I found the characterizations and performances rich. I get that you didn't, I'm just saying they're not objectively that way. 

> nothing about him is interesting beyond his childish behavior

Again, not saying you're wrong, it was your experience, just saying that I found him very interesting and there was a lot of depth there. He reminded me of people I've known in the past, people I worked with in the 80s and 90s. With dramas like this, it helps if you've had a lifetime of experiences to extrapolate from. There were movies I loved or hated at 30 that I had an opposite reaction to at 50. (Not trying to be condescending, but if you're younger, it may be hard to contextualize the film, like the proverbial anthropologist on Mars.)

I said the other day this is the most disappointing movie of the year for me. 

Visually it looks great and the performance of Adele Exarchpolous saved it from being utter trash (she really can’t do any wrong in my eyes) but there is so much to loathe about this film.

Without knowing anything about the director or having seen his previous films, this is clearly the work of an American liberal living out his bisexual European (maybe he says “Parisian” because he knows Europe isn’t a country) fantasies on film.  

Franz (whose surname I forget) plays the single most dislikable, unrelateable protagonist  who is so unbelievably up his own arse - I don’t care if you’re gay, I don’t care if you party in Berghain, you’re not wearing that ridiculous crop top to meet your pregnant girlfriend’s parents. 

British Ben was hilariously posh (again, the work of an American’s caricatured idea of a British creative/arty person). None of the men reacted to anything in a remotely believable way. 

I saw someone on Instagram say this should be called The Actual Worst Person In The World. I’d agree but Worst Film also fits.

The dialogue in the dining scene with the parents was laughable 

It was quite a heavy handed attempt from an American liberal to say “look at the values Europeans maintain which we lack”, everything that happens just feels a little too wild and unrealistic, like a very straight-laced person’s idea of a modern bohemian lifestyle 

Agree on the grading and photography, it looked beautiful. I’d actually go as far as to say it’s well acted, technically magnificent, but just atrociously written.
Did you feel like the movie was critical of the main character? I felt like it wasn’t and we were still supposed to sympathise with him which was odd as he was utterly awful
